textTitles: Willow Park playground — rules for users

paragraphs.text: Larkfield Health Centre — summer arrangements, July and August. The centre opens at 8 am and closes at 6.30 pm from Monday to Thursday, and at 1 pm on Fridays, when staff attend training. Telephone lines open at 8 am, and the busiest hour is the first one; if your matter is not urgent, calling after 11 am is easier. The centre is closed on public holidays, and the nearest walk-in service on those days is at Redhill, six kilometres away.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: Routine appointments are booked online or by telephone up to four weeks ahead. Urgent appointments are released each morning at 8 am and are given for the same day only; they are not held for later in the week. If you cannot come, cancel at least two hours before, so that the slot can be offered to someone else. Patients who miss three appointments in a year without cancelling will be written to, and may be asked to register elsewhere.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: Repeat prescriptions are ordered through the app or on the paper slip at reception, and take two working days, not counting the weekend. Please do not telephone to ask whether a prescription is ready; the pharmacy will send a message when it is. Blood tests are taken between 8.30 am and 11 am without an appointment, but the room closes when forty patients have been seen, which in July is usually before 10 am. Bring a form from the doctor; tests cannot be done without one.
paragraphs.label: C

texts.label: B
texts.title: Willow Park playground — rules for users

paragraphs.text: Willow Park playground — rules for users. The playground is open from 8 am until dusk and is for children up to twelve years old; the equipment is not designed for teenagers or adults and may be damaged by them. Every child under eight must be with someone aged fourteen or over. The gates must be kept shut, as the park is used by dogs, and dogs are not allowed inside the playground fence at any time, including on a lead.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: Food and drink may be brought in, but glass bottles may not, and bins are emptied on Monday and Thursday mornings. Bicycles and scooters are left at the rack by the gate rather than ridden inside. The surface under the climbing frame is inspected every fortnight by the council, and a piece of equipment with a red tag on it must not be used until the tag is removed. Please report damage using the number on the noticeboard rather than to the park café.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: The paddling pool runs from the last week of May to the first week of September and is filled on days when the forecast is above twenty degrees; it is emptied and cleaned every Tuesday, when it is closed all day. Organised groups of more than ten children need to book, and there is no charge for this. During school holidays a play worker is on site from 10 am to 2 pm on weekdays, and the sports court next to the playground may be used by older children at those hours.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: Goods in: receiving a delivery. Every delivery is checked against the purchase order before the driver leaves, and the driver is entitled to wait while you do it. Count the pallets first and compare the total with the delivery note; if the two disagree, write the number you counted on both copies and ask the driver to initial it. Never sign a note as "received unchecked" — the phrase has no meaning in a dispute and leaves the difference with us rather than with the supplier.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: Damage is treated separately from shortage. Visible damage is photographed at the tail of the lorry, before the pallet is moved, and written on the note in words as well as in the box provided. Hidden damage found later must be reported to the supplier within three working days, which is why pallets of glass and electrical goods are opened on the day they arrive rather than when they are needed. Keep the packaging of a damaged item until the claim is settled; suppliers routinely ask for it.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: Temperature-controlled deliveries have their own rule. Check the reading on the trailer display and write it on the note; if it is outside the range printed on the order, telephone the duty manager before unloading and do not put the goods into the chiller. A load refused at the door costs the supplier a delivery; a load accepted and then thrown away costs us the goods. The recorder in the trailer is downloaded by the driver and the printout is kept with our copy of the note.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: Once the delivery is accepted, book it into the system the same day, using the supplier code from the order rather than the name, since several suppliers trade under more than one name. Pallets go to the marked bay for their department, not to the nearest free space, and anything that has to be put away by hand is done before the end of the shift. If a delivery arrives after 4 pm and cannot be booked in, leave it in the holding bay with a card showing the date, and tell the next shift.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: Sickness absence: what to do. If you cannot come to work, telephone your line manager before the start of your shift, or as early as possible if you fall ill during the night. A message to a colleague, a text or an email does not count as notification unless your manager has agreed to it in advance. Say what is wrong in general terms and when you expect to return; you do not have to give a detailed diagnosis to anyone at work.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: For absences of up to seven calendar days you complete a self-certificate on your return, which is a single form signed by you and your manager. From the eighth day you need a fit note from a doctor, and if the absence continues, a new note before the last one expires. Send the note to the human resources inbox rather than to your department, and keep a copy; the original is not returned to you.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: Pay during sickness follows length of service. Staff with less than a year receive statutory pay only; after one year the company pays full salary for up to four weeks in any twelve-month period, and half salary for four weeks after that. Absence that is caused by an accident at work is paid in full from the first day regardless of service, and the accident must also be recorded in the accident book on the day it happens.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: Returning is easier when it is planned. After an absence of more than two weeks your manager will hold a short return-to-work meeting, which is a conversation rather than a disciplinary step; its purpose is to agree what, if anything, needs to change. Adjustments such as shorter days, different duties or a later start can be agreed for a fixed period and are reviewed at the end of it. If you are unwell again within eight weeks with the same condition, the absences are treated as one for the purposes of pay.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: The school meal began as a response to hunger rather than as an idea about nutrition. In the first decades of the twentieth century, teachers in industrial cities reported that children arrived unable to concentrate, and charities began serving soup in classrooms. Governments followed slowly and unevenly, and in most countries the meal became universal only when a war made the health of children a matter of state interest. That origin explains a good deal about what followed: the service was designed to fill, cheaply, and everything else was added later.
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: For thirty years after the middle of the century, the school meal was treated as solved. Kitchens were built in schools, cooks were employed by the education authority, and a hot dinner was served to everyone who wanted it at a price the state largely covered. The food was plain and repetitive, but it was cooked on site from raw ingredients, and the children ate the same thing at the same time, which schools valued for reasons that had nothing to do with food.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: The change came from accounting rather than from cooking. When school budgets were devolved and catering was put out to tender, the contract went to whoever could deliver the meal for the lowest price, and the cheapest way to deliver a meal is to buy it ready-made and reheat it. Kitchens were converted into servery counters, cooks became servers, and the menu moved towards items that survive a warming cabinet. Nobody decided that children should eat worse; a series of separate decisions about cost made it very likely that they would.
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: The reaction, when it came, was driven by television rather than by research. A series of programmes in the mid-2000s showed what was on the plate, and the public response was strong enough that several governments introduced binding standards: limits on fried food and sugar, a required portion of vegetables, restrictions on what could be sold in vending machines. Studies of schools that met the standards found measurable improvements — more vegetables eaten, better concentration in the afternoon, and, in some datasets, better results in national tests.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: Getting children to eat the improved food turned out to be a second problem. Standards govern what is served, not what is swallowed, and early evaluations found a good deal of it in the bin. What changed that was unglamorous: longer lunch breaks, because a child with fifteen minutes will eat the pudding first; dining rooms that are not also the gymnasium; enough serving points that the queue does not consume the break; and letting children see the food before they choose. Schools that fixed the queue often improved intake more than schools that changed the recipes.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: The question of who pays has never been settled. Where meals are free for everyone, take-up is high and the stigma of a free meal disappears, but the cost is large and falls on education budgets that are already tight. Where meals are free only for poorer families, a proportion of eligible children do not claim, either because the application is complicated or because they do not want to be identified. Trials of universal provision consistently raise take-up among exactly the children the targeted scheme was meant to reach, which is an argument that money alone does not settle.
paragraphs.label: F

paragraphs.text: What a meal is for has widened again. Schools now use lunch to teach eating as a social act, to introduce foods that families may not buy, and, in a growing number of countries, to reduce waste and to shorten supply chains by buying locally. Some of this is measurable and some is not; a child who tries a vegetable at school and asks for it at home is a real effect that no evaluation captures. The risk in the widening is the old one: a service asked to do six things at once, with a budget calculated for one.
paragraphs.label: G

paragraphs.text: The history is therefore less a story of progress than of repeated rediscovery. Almost everything that works now — cooking on site, eating together, enough time, food that children have seen being made — was normal in 1960 and was given up for reasons that were about money rather than about children. That is worth remembering, because the pressure that removed those things has not gone away, and the standards that brought some of them back are only as durable as the budget behind them.
paragraphs.label: H
